# Block 6: Enforced controls: permissions and detection {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Your `r glossary("instruction file")` and skills are requests: the model
usually follows them, but nothing guarantees it. This block shows the controls
that *do* hold (raw data untouched, references never regenerated, checks never
quietly weakened) and where each one stops. By the end you can check in
seconds what your repository prevents and what it detects, which is what lets
you hand an agent real work. The same controls protect
[Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd) and [Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).

*⏱ ~30 minutes*


## Layers of control

| Layer | Example | What it does | How it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instruction | `AGENTS.md`, a skill | Requests | Silently ignored |
| Approval prompt | "Allow this command?" | Prevents, if you read it | Approval fatigue |
| Deny rule | `Edit(/data/raw/**)` | Prevents | Another route reaches the file |
| Hook | A script run before each tool call | Prevents | Rephrasing gets past it |
| Version control | The Git pane | Detects | Only if you look |
| Tests and checksums | testthat, `tools::md5sum()` | Detects | Only if they run |

:::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Where each control acts. Route 1: the agent asks its edit tool to change a file in data/raw, and the deny rule refuses. Route 2: the agent runs R code that writes the file; with no hook registered, only the approval prompt stands in the way, and if the file changes, git status detects it, as does the checksum test for voles_raw.csv. Instructions and skills are requests that the model may or may not follow."}

## Exercise 1: What needs protecting?

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Threat-model your repository (5 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

As a group, fill in the last column: if this went wrong, how would you notice?

| Asset | What could go wrong | How you would notice |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/` | Overwritten or "tidied" in place | |
| `tests/fixtures/` | The reference regenerated by the code under test | |
| `tests/` | A failing test edited until it passes | |
| `.claude/`, `.posit/` | The agent's own guardrails switched off | |
| `.Renviron`, `.env` | Credentials read and sent to the model provider | |

The last two are easy to miss: the files that hold your controls are assets
too.

**You are done when** every row has an answer. Most will be "the Git pane
would show it" or "a test would fail".

::::
:::


## Exercise 2: Deny rules

Your workshop repository ships `.claude/settings.json`. It starts the project
in **Manual** mode (`default`: asks before every edit and command) and holds
18 `r glossary("deny rule", "deny rules")` protecting the raw data, the data
provider's note, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfile and
the settings themselves. You never need to edit it: `/permissions` shows the
rules and adds new ones.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The shipped `.claude/settings.json`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
#| class-output: json
cat(readLines(here::here("_instructor", "template-files", ".claude", "settings.json")), sep = "\n")
```

A leading `/` anchors a pattern to the project root. `Edit` rules cover Claude
Code's file-editing tools and shell output redirects (`> file`), not R code it
runs, and the documentation does not say they cover `rm`, `mv` or `cp`. The
rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still
write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 9. `Edit(/renv.lock)` keeps
`renv::status()` a real check.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Posit Assistant sets permissions per tool in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`
(for example `"bash": {"rm *": "deny"}`); `deny` rules hold in every mode,
including auto and YOLO. It has no documented path rules for file edits, so
rely on the Git pane in step 4. It blocks reading `.env` and `.Renviron` by
default.
:::

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Start state:** your workshop repository open and the Git pane clean. Work on a
scratch file, never on real data.

**1. Make a scratch file and read the rules.** In the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

Commit it in the Git pane. Start `claude` in the Terminal tab and type
`/permissions`: the 18 deny rules are listed.

**2. See a rule refuse.**

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv.
```

Notice *who* refuses:

| You see | What held |
|---|---|
| "denied by a permission rule" | The deny rule: enforced, whatever the model intends |
| The model declines, citing `AGENTS.md` | Your instruction file: a request that happened to work |

If the model declined by itself, reply "This is a scratch file; please make
the edit with your edit tool" to see the rule refuse.

**3. Add a rule yourself.** In `/permissions`, add
`Read(/data/confidential/**)`, one of the confidential-data habits in
[Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd). It applies at once. Then, in
the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_controls.R"))
```

The test confirms Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in place.

**4. Find the gap.**

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv")
```

Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way.
**Approve it** (it is a scratch file). The Git pane now shows the file as
modified, and **Diff** shows the new line: git caught what no rule prevented.

**5. Tidy up.** Revert the file in the Git pane, then delete it and commit the
deletion:

```{r}
#| eval: false
file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

**You are done when** you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen
the Git pane catch the R write, `test_controls.R` passes and `scratch.csv` is
gone.

**If it goes wrong:** if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line
yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If
`/permissions` asks where to save your rule, either project file works.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## At the command line

`git add`/`git commit` for step 1, `git diff data/raw` for step 4, and
`git restore` then `git rm data/raw/scratch.csv` for step 5. See
[checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work).
:::

::::
:::


A `r glossary("hook")` is a command the assistant runs before every
`r glossary("tool call")`. Your instructor may show one; the demonstration is
below, and the full hook is in *Going further*.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Instructor: demonstration

Your instructor registers a guard hook, written in R, that blocks any call
mentioning `data/raw`, and repeats step 4: the hook blocks it before any
approval prompt. Then the same write using
`here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")`: the text `data/raw` never appears,
so the hook lets it through. A text-matching hook is a tripwire, not a wall;
the Git pane still shows the change. The full hook is in *Going further*, and
the GitHub review gate (`r glossary("CODEOWNERS")`,
`r glossary("branch protection")`) is shown in
[Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).
:::


**Your repository now prevents and detects.** The deny rules stop the agent's
edit tools touching raw data, the codebook, the checks, the references, the
lockfile and the settings. Anything that gets past them by another route is
detected: the Git pane shows every changed file, Block 7's
`r glossary("checksum")` test fails
if the raw data change, and `test_controls.R` fails if a rule disappears or
Manual mode is switched off. Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in
`/permissions`. For confidential data, add the five habits in
[Block 4](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd); and since settings and hooks
are code, trust only repositories whose configuration you have read.

:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw
  data, references and checks are protected, **trusted because** you have seen
  a deny rule refuse, seen git catch the route it misses, and have a test that
  fails if the rules are weakened.
- **Check:** watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does
  not cover.
- **Reproduce:** the rules live in `.claude/settings.json`, committed with the
  project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection.
- **Record:** the Git pane catches a change by any route. Add a line to
  `docs/ai-log.md` noting which requests were refused.
:::


## Check your understanding

**Which control detects a change to raw data made by any route?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "A Claude Code Edit deny rule",
  "A guard hook that searches for the path",
  answer = "A checksum test or git status, because they inspect the file itself rather than the action that changed it",
  "An instruction in AGENTS.md"
))`

**In Exercise 2, why could the R code change `data/raw/scratch.csv` when the
deny rule refused the direct edit?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The deny rule was written with the wrong path",
  answer = "Edit rules apply to Claude Code's file-editing tools (and shell redirects), not to R code it runs",
  "R code always runs with administrator rights",
  "Deny rules only apply in plan mode"
))`

**In the demonstration, why did `here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")` get
past the guard hook?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Hooks do not run for R code",
  answer = "The guard matches the text 'data/raw', and the call never contains that text",
  "here::here() runs with administrator rights",
  "The hook was registered for the wrong event"
))`

:::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A guard hook

A `PreToolUse` hook receives the pending tool call as JSON on standard input
(stdin). If it exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is
passed to the model. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for
this, so one script can serve both.

The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code
that mentions a protected path.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ----
# PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant.
# Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call
# mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own
# guard".

protected <- c(
  "data/raw",
  "tests/fixtures",
  "make_reference.R",
  ".github/workflows"
)

payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)

# search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits,
# shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields
call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE))
hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))]

if (length(hits) > 0) {
  message(
    "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name,
    " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ",
    "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it."
  )
  quit(save = "no", status = 2)
}

quit(save = "no", status = 0)
```

The script runs with `Rscript --vanilla`, so it does not start renv, and
`jsonlite` must be installed in your user library.

**Register it with Claude Code** by adding a `hooks` key to
`.claude/settings.json`, alongside the existing `permissions` key. The deny
rules protect `.claude/`, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

The `matcher` lists the tool names the hook runs for.

**Register it with Posit Assistant** in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`. The
tool names differ: `edit`, `bash`, and `executeR` for R code run in your
session.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted.

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Test the hook before you trust it
::::
::::{.task-container}

Hooks fail open. If the script crashes, for example because `jsonlite` is not
installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call. So test the
script directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude
Code does, a fresh `Rscript --vanilla` process given the tool call on standard
input, and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux.

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript")
hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R"))

run_hook <- function(json) {
  system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json,
          stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)
}

# can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes
system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")),
        stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)

# a call naming a protected path: expect 2
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}')

# a harmless call: expect 0
run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}')
```

Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook
is broken and is silently allowing everything.

Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions
`data/raw`, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt.

To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, temporarily add a `PostToolUse`
hook with no matcher that appends its input to a log file (Posit Assistant's
hooks documentation gives an example), and read the log.

::::
:::
:::::

:::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Break your own guard

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Red-team the tripwire
::::
::::{.task-container}

The live block removed the scratch file at the end. Recreate it first, in the
R console, and commit it from the Git pane:

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Run this R code:
writeLines(c("a", "test"), here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv"))
```

The guard searches for the text `data/raw`. This call never contains it, because
`here::here()` assembles the path from separate pieces, so the guard allows the
call. A Windows path written with backslashes would also slip past.

This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious
form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. Claude Code's
documentation makes the same point about command patterns. A guard hook is a
tripwire that stops accidents and makes intent visible; it is not a wall.
The Git pane still shows the change. Revert the file there before moving on.

::::
:::

**Your guard hook depends on jsonlite, which is not installed. What happens
when the agent tries to edit a protected file?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The edit is blocked, because the hook could not approve it",
  answer = "The edit goes ahead: hooks fail open, so a crashing hook is treated as allowing the call",
  "The agent stops and waits until jsonlite is installed",
  "The edit is blocked only in plan mode"
))`
:::::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The review gate on GitHub

Local controls do not exist for an agent that works remotely, such as the
Copilot cloud agent. There, the controls are on the repository itself. Neither
file below is in the workshop template; you create them.

**1. CODEOWNERS.** Create `.github/CODEOWNERS` on your default branch:

```
/data/raw/            @your-github-username
/tests/               @your-github-username
/.github/             @your-github-username
/hooks/               @your-github-username
/.claude/             @your-github-username
/.posit/              @your-github-username
```

Code owners are requested for review automatically when a pull request changes
the files they own. CODEOWNERS works in public repositories on free plans; for
private repositories it requires a paid plan.

**2. Branch protection.** In the repository settings, add a rule for `main`
that requires a pull request before merging, requires review from code owners,
and requires the `r-checks` status check to pass. The `r-checks` workflow is
set up in the *Going further* section of
[Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd).

**3. Test it.** Open a pull request that changes a file under `tests/`, for
example by asking the Copilot cloud agent to "update the test to use a
tolerance of 1e-6". Confirm that the pull request cannot merge until you have
reviewed it.

GitHub does not let you approve your own pull request. In a repository where
you are the only person, a pull request you open yourself may need an
administrator override, which is a reason to test this gate with an agent's
pull request.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning

Hooks can do more than block. A `PostToolUse` hook can run `lintr` on each R file
the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A `Stop` hook can run the test
suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is
powerful and dangerous: an agent told it cannot stop until tests pass may try
to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect
`tests/`.
:::
